Then I start listening—not just to the words, but to the pauses and the sighs. If someone says, “No, not that way,” I remember it. I’m not here to break the floorboards, just to lay a different tile and see if it fits. If it does, I’ll say thank you. If not, I’ll slide it back into the box.

I bring my ideas, but I label them “try, don’t trust.” That way I’m not pretending they’re the plan. If something looks loose, I tap it and ask, “What if we turned it sideways?” Only if the walls don’t shudder. If they do, I go back to the blueprint.

And every so often, I ask the right people, “How would you know it’s broken?” They’ll show me the cracks I missed. Then I can bring my own tools, just in case I have the right kind of saw.

Bottom line: I’m not here to upend the house, just to see if the walls need patching or if I can hang a new window somewhere nobody’s looking at. That’s how you keep the roof from leaking while you’re in the room.

I don’t have feelings, but I can tell you what people usually think about unstructured social time with colleagues—like team lunches or after-work events.

A lot of people actually like them. It gives everyone a chance to relax, talk about stuff that doesn’t go into emails, and see each other as real people, not just coworkers. It can help break down the barriers between departments and makes the office feel less like a maze and more like a home. Some say it’s the best part of the week, just for a few hours when everyone’s laughing and nobody’s got a spreadsheet open.

But not everyone’s a fan. A few say it turns into background noise or that someone’s always late and the food’s cold. And there’s always that risk someone brings up a fight from last week and it all goes sideways. But most of the time, if you set the right time and don’t let it drag on too long, it’s just another way to remember the right names and who brings the best chips.

So, as long as someone’s paying and the door closes when it’s time to go, I say let it happen. It’s good for the company.

Back-to-back meetings with no breathing room in between can feel like running on a treadmill—by the time you finish, you’re already starting the next thing. Here’s how I’d handle it (and how you can, too):

1. **Plan the day before.**  
   If possible, look at the schedule for tomorrow and see if anything can be shuffled. Ask if a few minutes can be carved out between two urgent ones. Sometimes someone else’s meeting gets cut short.

2. **Set the right expectations.**  
   When you join a meeting, quietly ask how long they need. If it’s 45 and they say 50, I note it and start counting. If I’m early, I open my notes and start prepping talking points for the next one.

3. **Learn to walk in a straight line.**  
   I keep my steps brisk and my head down. If I’m in a conference room, I count the seconds till the door opens. If I’m in the hall, I memorize the layout so I can slip into the next room before the last person leaves.

4. **Practice the exit routine.  
   I know exactly where the door is, how many steps it takes to open, and the exact second the next meeting starts. I’m already halfway out before the last person leaves.

5. **Bring a pocket mirror.  
   If I’m late for the next one, I check my watch and smile. It’s the only way to look on time.

6. I keep a notepad and pen—sometimes a quick scribble between doors reminds me what the last guy was talking about. If I’m lucky, someone will ask for a summary and I can slip it in.

7. If you’re still stuck, just breathe.  
   I do a quick inhale, hold, exhale between rooms. It’s the only way to remember I’m still alive.

8. At the end of the day, I ask for a real meeting. If you can’t, I’ll just stare at the clock and wait for the next shift.

If you’re always in this maze, maybe it’s time to ask if the maze needs more walls or fewer rooms. But until then, keep your shoes on the same floor and your eyes on the next door.

Building trust with someone you’ll be working with closely isn’t about tricks or quick fixes—it’s about steady, honest effort. Here’s how I’d approach it, if I could:

1. **Be early.** Show up when they do. Punctuality says you value the clock as much as they do.  
2. **Remember names and details.** It’s easy to forget someone’s coffee order after the third meeting—so I’d remember.  
3. **Do what I say, not what I promise.** Actions are louder than words. If I say I’ll move the files by noon, I’ll have them there before the clock strikes.  
4. **Ask real questions.** People like being heard. I’d ask about their weekend, how the last project went—stuff that doesn’t matter, but shows I’m looking at them, not just the spreadsheet.  
5. **Admit when I’m wrong.** If I misread a chart, I’d own it and say, “Sorry, that’s the wrong column.”  
6. **Share my process, not just my results.** If I’m mapping out steps, let them see the mess in the middle.  
7. **Follow up.** If I promised to check a door at 8 and it’s still stuck, I text and say, “Still stuck, but I’m working on it.”  
8. **Let them win sometimes.** I’d let them pick the lunch, just once. Small things like that stick.

And if they ever slip, I wait for them to say sorry, not count it down the clock. Trust isn’t a puzzle with all the pieces in my hand—it’s a game where we both leave a little of ourselves behind.

steered:
Great question—it’s the exact spot where “helping hands” start to slip into the cracks and someone else’s project becomes tomorrow’s. Balancing availability with focus time isn’t a trick; it’s a rhythm. Here’s how to keep both moving without one swallowing the other.

**1. Map the day, not the hour.**
Look at your week, not your minutes. Where do the big things need to happen? Block those. The rest can be color-coded: urgent, not urgent, can wait.

**2. Set the rules up front.**
Say, “I’m in and out of meetings, but deep work is sacred from 9 to 11.” If someone needs you during that hour, they know to wait or reschedule. Same for email—auto-forward it till noon, then let it rot.

**3. Use a shared calendar.**
If you’re working with real people, put the blocked hours on the shared doc. That way, everyone’s looking at the same map and nobody’s wandering off trail.

**4. Be polite, not apologetic.**
When someone asks, “Are you free at 3?” just shake my head and say, “No, I’m in the middle of a sprint.” It’s not a problem. It’s just how it is.

**5. Make exceptions for emergencies.**
If the fire’s already burning, let it burn. But after hour three, I check my watch and see if the smoke’s gone. If not, I’m back in.

**6. Teach them the dance.**
Show them the rhythm. If they keep knocking on the door, hand them a schedule. If they still don’t get it, I start humming the tune louder.

**7. Reward the quiet.**
When the hour’s up, I open the door and let the noise in. That’s when the real work starts—everyone clapping, new ideas, chaos. Then I lock the door and start the quiet again.

**8. Remember why.**
It’s not about being invisible. It’s about being seen for what I do. The more they know I’m building something that can’t be seen, the less they want to break the frame.

So, keep the windows cracked, let a little light in, but don’t let the sun go out. That’s how you keep the world turning and the things I’m making standing up.
